“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father, and you, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the greatest impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” Wemmick replied, growing bolder still. “I think you’re the other one.”

Once again they exchanged their strange looks, each apparently still unsure whether the other was making fun of him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it be so. Now, looking at you, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you were planning and arranging to have a pleasant home of your own one day, when you’ve grown tired of all this work.”

{"request_id":"f4884ea00c389a39c1e10148","rewritten_text":"I am very ignorant, and it troubles me—just a little.”

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative and an orphan like me, whom I love very dearly. She is five years younger than I am, and she lives in a farmer’s house in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has happened to me—for I cannot write—and even if I could, how could I tell her? It is better this way.”

“Yes, yes: better this way.”

“What I was thinking as we came here, and what I am still thinking as I look into your kind, strong face, which gives me so much comfort, is this: If the Republic truly helps the poor, and they become less hungry and suffer less in every way, she may live for a long time. She may even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think”—the calm eyes, filled with so much endurance, fill with tears, and her lips part a little farther and tremble—“that the time will seem long to me while I wait for her in the better land, where I trust that both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot be, my child; there is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much! I am so ignorant. Am I to kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers; they solemnly bless each other. His free hand does not tremble as he lets hers go; nothing worse than a sweet, bright calm remains in the patient face. She goes before him—she is gone; the knitting-women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.”

The murmur of many voices, the lifting of many faces, and the press of many feet at the edge of the crowd, causing it to surge forward like one great wave of water, all vanish in a flash. Twenty-Three.

It is dreadful enough, though it lasts only about five minutes. Then the curtain goes up, and you will see the girl to whom I am going to devote my whole life, to whom I have given everything good within me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid a remarkable uproar of applause, Sibyl Vane came onto the stage. Yes, she was undeniably beautiful to behold—one of the loveliest beings Lord Henry had ever seen. There was something fawnlike in her timid grace and startled eyes. A delicate blush, like the reflection of a rose upon silver, touched her cheeks as she looked toward the crowded, excited audience. She retreated a few steps, and her lips appeared to quiver. Basil Hallward sprang up and began clapping. Dorian Gray sat still, as though dreaming, staring at her. Lord Henry looked through his spectacles and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene represented the hall of Capulet’s house, and Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other companions. The band, such as it was, played a few measures, and the dance commenced. Among the crowd of awkward, poorly dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a being from a more beautiful world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant moving beneath water. The lines of her throat resembled those of a white lily. Her hands seemed fashioned from cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely languid. When her eyes fell upon Romeo, she showed no trace of happiness. The few lines she had to speak—

{"request_id":"4acf743273c4a628ec523f","rewritten_text":"‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he really is some kind of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I hope he is a foreigner, at least. That would make it rather less unpleasant.’

‘I must certainly present him to you.’

‘Present him!’ exclaimed the Duchess. ‘You don’t mean that he is here?’ She began searching for a little tortoiseshell fan and a very ragged lace shawl, ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here; I should never think of giving a party without him. He says that I have a perfectly psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even slightly shorter, I would have become a confirmed pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I understand!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘Misfortunes as well,’ replied Lady Windermere, ‘and in enormous quantities. Next year, for example, I am in serious danger on both land and sea, so I intend to live in a balloon and have my dinner hauled up to me in a basket every evening. It is all written on my little finger—or perhaps in the palm of my hand; I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence is capable of resisting temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their hands read once a month, simply to learn what they should avoid doing. Naturally, one does it anyway, but being warned is so agreeable. Now, if someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Allow me to go, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man who stood nearby, listening to the conversation with an amused smile.

‘Thank you very much, Lord Arthur; but I am afraid you would not know him.’

‘If he is as remarkable as you claim, Lady Windermere, I could hardly fail to find him. Describe him to me, and I will bring him here at once.’

‘Well, he does not resemble a chiromantist in the least. I mean, he is neither mysterious, nor esoteric, nor romantic in appearance. He is a short, stout man with an amusing bald head and enormous gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country solicitor. I am truly sorry, but it is not my fault. People are so irritating. All my pianists look precisely like poets, and all my poets look precisely like pianists. I remember last season inviting a most terrible conspirator to dinner, a man who had blown up countless people, always wore a coat of mail, and carried a dagger up his sleeve; and do you know, when he arrived, he looked exactly like a pleasant old clergyman and spent the whole evening telling jokes?’"}
